questions: Does oval progress rise above 0.38 with the 0.035 m wheels, and does the speed gain translate into more distance covered before the off-track end?
Does steering_oscillation stay at or below about 0.2 on the oval, or does the larger wheel raise yaw gain per command?
Does max_error move below 0.06 m, or does it stay at 0.061 to 0.064 m? If it stays, is the controller gain the only remaining limit?
Is there any completion on any track, or any run that reaches progress above 0.6 on the s-bend or slalom?

intent: Test the speed lever in isolation. Raise wheel_radius from 0.030 to 0.035 m and hold everything else at iteration 5: 7 sensors at y = 0.02 m, x = ±0.06 m, 16 mm footprints, 0.10 m track, 0.8 kg mass and 0.16 m body. Expected: oval progress rises from 0.36 toward 0.40 or more, line_loss_events stays at 0, oval steering_oscillation stays at or below about 0.2, and max_error stays near 0.062 m. If oscillation rises above 0.2, the wheel-radius yaw gain is the cause and the next move is a wider track of 0.11 m.
learning: Iteration 5 confirmed that the reaction point at y = 0.02 m removes slalom line loss and keeps oscillation under 0.2, but max_error stays at 0.062 m. Geometry does not move the off-track floor, so the next geometry change targets speed (wheel radius). If progress rises and oscillation holds, the next geometry step is to tune speed further or to hand the remaining max_error gap to the Integrator as a controller problem.
rationale: Evidence from iteration 5 (y = 0.02 m row, otherwise iteration 4): line loss is now 0 on all three tracks, including the slalom, which had 0.25 events at y = 0.03 m. Oval steering_oscillation fell to 0.193, still under the 0.2 threshold. Oval progress rose to 0.358, which clears the Integrator's 0.35 trigger for a speed test, though only just. Max_error is still 0.0622 m on every track, so the row move did not change the off-track floor. Across iterations 0 to 5 max_error has stayed at 0.061 to 0.064 m whatever the track width, mass, footprint or row height. Body width cannot lift the floor, because max(0.06, 0.0125 + body_width/4) stays at 0.06 m for every allowed body width. My conclusion is that geometry has little left to offer for max_error. The remaining geometry lever is speed, which governs whether the robot can finish the course within 3 s. Oval progress of 0.36 in 3 s is far short of completion. Wheel radius is the speed lever: ground speed scales with radius at a given wheel rotation rate. Changing wheel radius from 0.030 to 0.035 m raises speed by about 17 percent. I am keeping mass at 0.8 kg and body 0.16 m, because lowering mass to 0.7 kg would cut yaw inertia toward the range where oscillation rose above 0.2 in iterations 2 and 3. This keeps the test to a single speed change with the sensor row at y = 0.02 m, 16 mm footprints and the seven-sensor span. The risk is that a larger wheel gives more yaw per command, which could push oscillation back above 0.2. Expected result: oval progress rises to about 0.40 to 0.42, line loss stays at 0, and max_error stays near 0.062 m. Completion becomes possible only if progress keeps rising on the held-back tracks.
